precepts.text: For we know that the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now. And not only they, but ourselves also, which have the firstfruits of the Spirit, which is Christ: waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body. We want our godhood back. We want rulership back, dominion back; we want to reign on this planet like we once did.
precepts.point: To loose those that are appointed to death: he said he is going to loose those appointed to death.

note.label: Job Sees America's 250th Anniversary

precepts.why:
Solomon saw “the tears of such as were oppressed, and they had no comforter; and on the side of their oppressors there was power.” They have the guns, the nuclear weapons, the court system; they have it all, and we have nothing. But the psalm says the Lord looked down from heaven “To hear the groaning of the prisoner; to loose those that are appointed to death.” We are the prisoner. You know what it is like to be the son of God and be in prison: in a weak body, ruled and dominated by a wicked race of people, subject to their laws.

Paul hears the same groaning: “For we know that the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now.” Just like we groan, all creation groans.

“And not only they, but ourselves also, which have the firstfruits of the Spirit”: the firstfruits of the Spirit is Christ. “even we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body.”

That redemption of the body is what the prisoner groans for. We want our godhood back. We want rulership back, dominion back; we want to reign on this planet like we once did. That is the loosing of those appointed to death that the Lord looked down from heaven to bring.

precepts.text: This is His name forever and His memorial unto all generations: the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
precepts.point: But the Most High shall endure forever and His remembrance unto all generations. That remembrance is that He is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

note.label: Psalm 102: Hear My Prayer, O Lord

precepts.why:
“But thou, O Lord, shalt endure for ever; and thy remembrance unto all generations.” Man's days are like a shadow that declines, withered like grass, but the Most High endures forever. That remembrance is that he is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

He said so to Moses: “Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, The Lord God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, hath sent me unto you: this is my name for ever, and this is my memorial unto all generations.” This is his name forever and his memorial unto all generations: the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

The remembrance unto all generations in Psalm 102 is the memorial unto all generations in Exodus 3. The Most High endures forever as the God of our fathers.

precepts.text: When the Most High builds up Zion he regards the prayer of the destitute and the groaning of the prisoner, which is Israel.
precepts.point: Israel were the prisoners of Rome, the oppressed, and the Most High hears the prayer of the oppressed, not the prayer of the oppressor. Salvation coming up as a memorial belongs to Zion and to Jerusalem, not to the captor.

note.label: Acts 10: Cornelius and the Northern Kingdom Grafted In

precepts.why:
The angel told Cornelius, “Thy prayers and thine alms are come up for a memorial before God.” The Most High only regards the prayer of Zion, of the destitute, of the prisoner, so his hearing Cornelius marks Cornelius as Israel.

“When the Lord shall build up Zion, he shall appear in his glory. He will regard the prayer of the destitute, and not despise their prayer.” And he looks down from heaven “To hear the groaning of the prisoner; to loose those that are appointed to death.”

Israel were the prisoners of Rome, the oppressed. The Most High hears the prayer of the oppressed, not the prayer of the oppressor. Salvation coming up as a memorial belongs to Zion and to Jerusalem, not to the captor.

note.label: Job Sees America's 250th Anniversary

points: He shortened my days. Thy years are throughout all generations: God's years go throughout all generations. The generations there are not talking about each kid; it is talking about different societies and times.

So back in Genesis 15: they will be afflicted four hundred years, and in the fourth generation they come back to the land. In this context, how many years is one generation? A hundred years. The generation there is societal generation, every hundred years, because the Most High gives most people seventy years to live, eighty with strength. Within a hundred years society changes and everybody you know is dead. Them four hundred years is four generations. We came back into the land under Moses and Joshua, about four hundred thirty years after.

note.label: The Plagues Coming to America

points: They shall perish, but thou shalt endure: the generations perish. All of them shall wax old like a garment; as a vesture shalt thou change them, and they shall be changed. Generations change. At one point of time the Babylonians ruled this earth, then the Persians, then the Greeks; at one point Britain ruled the earth, and now America rules the earth. Those were different time frames and different generations.

note.label: The Plagues Coming to America

points: But thou art the same, and thy years shall have no end: God does not change.
